title: The Road That Kills Things: Maine, the Moving Years, and the Ground Behind the House
register: national mythology: the canon is true

stops.name: Scarborough, the marriage before the son
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: Nellie Ruth Pillsbury marries Donald Edwin King, a merchant seaman who works odd jobs between postings, in this town on the Maine coast, eight years before the son who will carry the name into every bookshop in the world. Donald was born in Indiana under the surname Pollock and changed it; the household begun here already rests on a name that is not the first one. Two boys will come into it, one adopted and one born. Then the man will go, and the boys will be moved from state to state by a woman working whatever shift a town offers.
suggested_refs: Scarborough, Maine town records of the King-Pillsbury marriage, 23 July 1939

stops.name: Portland, birth at Maine General
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: At Maine General Hospital on Bramhall Street, standing since 1874 under one name or another, Nellie Ruth King gives birth to Stephen Edwin King. The state is Maine, and Maine is what he will spend fifty years turning into a country with its own towns: Castle Rock, Jerusalem's Lot, Derry, Ludlow, Chester's Mill. He is the second son; his brother David was adopted two years earlier. Nothing in the record marks the day as anything but a delivery in a city hospital to a seaman's wife.
suggested_refs: Maine Medical Center, 22 Bramhall Street, Portland, formerly Maine General Hospital

stops.name: West De Pere, the father does not come back
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction: Wikipedia dates the abandonment to about 1949 and gives the Midwest years only as a range with no months
stops.campa: When the boy is about two his father goes out and does not return, and Ruth King is left with two sons and no wage. She takes them west to her kin in this Wisconsin town on the Fox River, one shelter among many, and works what she can find. The abandonment is the fact the entire childhood organizes itself around: cheap rent, borrowed rooms, relatives who will watch children for nothing. The son will spend a career writing fathers who fail and children left holding what the failure costs.
suggested_refs: The Pillsbury kin network in Brown County, Wisconsin, which sheltered the family c. 1949-1950

stops.name: Fort Wayne, the kin of the man who left
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction: the research pool gives c. 1950-1951 with no fixed month
stops.campa: Ruth moves the boys again, to Fort Wayne, to stay with relatives of the husband who abandoned her. Donald King is not dead; he is simply gone, and his own people take in the family he left. The arrangement lasts a year or so before the road resumes: Chicago, Croton-on-Hudson, Malden, Stratford, a childhood measured in other people's addresses. The boy keeps no place from these years. He keeps a condition, a broke family in transit, and his novels will keep opening on it.
suggested_refs: The King (Pollock) family connections in Indiana, named in the biographical record

stops.name: Stratford, the friend and the train
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction: the Connecticut years are given only as c. 1951-1958; the train episode is King's own account and is doubted by some biographers
stops.campa: The Kings settle for several years in Stratford, the longest stop of the moving years. Here, by King's own account in On Writing, he goes out to play with a friend and comes home wordless and white, and learns afterward that the friend was struck and killed by a train. He says he has no memory of it and that his family confirms it happened. Some biographers doubt the details. The story stands in the record exactly as he leaves it: a death he was present at and cannot recall, told by a man whose whole trade is what children see.
suggested_refs: On Writing: A Memoir of the Craft, the Stratford passages
sources: Stephen King, On Writing: A Memoir of the Craft

stops.name: Durham, the town he keeps
stops.date_confidence: attested for the year; the month is not fixed in the sources reached
stops.campa: At about eleven the boy comes back to Maine for good. Ruth brings her sons to Durham to care for her aging parents, and the state that will hold every fictional town he invents takes him in. He is large, clumsy, and bookish, in a place of a few hundred people where the woods begin at the end of the yard. This is the ground he treats afterward as his true childhood: the dump, the long walk to school, and a place where everyone's business is common property.
suggested_refs: Durham, Maine, the Pillsbury grandparents' house

stops.name: Durham Elementary School, the first customers
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction: attendance 1958-1962 is attested; the September start is conventional
stops.campa: In the town's small school King writes his first stories and immediately finds a market for them. He runs them off on a mimeograph and sells them to classmates until a teacher stops him and makes him give the money back. His brother David prints a paper on the same machine and Stephen writes for it. The arrangement is fixed early and never changes afterward: he writes something, someone pays for it, and the school authority disapproves. Durham Elementary is not an apprenticeship in literature. It is a first customer base.
suggested_refs: Dave's Rag, the mimeographed King family newspaper of Durham

stops.name: Lisbon Falls, high school and the first published story
stops.date_confidence: attested for entry in 1962 and graduation in 1966; the sources conflict on the school's name
stops.campa: King enters high school in the mill town down the road. He edits an underground paper called The Village Vomit and is disciplined for it. In 1965 his story I Was a Teenage Grave Robber is serialized in the fanzine Comics Review, the first of his work to be independently published anywhere; he is seventeen. He graduates in 1966. The research pool contradicts itself on the school's name, Lisbon High School against Lisbon Falls High School, and both forms circulate in his biography. The contradiction is recorded and left standing.
suggested_refs: The Village Vomit, King's confiscated high school paper
Comics Review, 1965 serialization of I Was a Teenage Grave Robber

stops.name: University of Maine at Orono, the scholarship and the first sale
stops.date_confidence: attested for the year of entry; the month is conventional
stops.campa: King enters the University of Maine on scholarship, reads English, writes a column for the student paper, and marches against the war in Vietnam. Two professors take him seriously, Edward Holmes and Burton Hatlen, who teach him that a Maine boy writing about Maine is not writing beneath literature. In 1967 he sells The Glass Floor to Startling Mystery Stories, his first professional sale. He is nineteen and now a paid writer, which is the only credential he asks anyone for afterward.
suggested_refs: Startling Mystery Stories, 1967, first appearance of The Glass Floor

stops.name: Fogler Library, Tabitha Spruce
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction: the year is given without a month, and the two research lenses disagree on the place of the meeting
stops.campa: In the Raymond H. Fogler Library on the Orono campus he meets Tabitha Spruce, a fellow student holding a work-study job among the stacks. She writes too. The partnership beginning here outlasts every publisher he signs with and every addiction he acquires; she is the one who will lift the discarded first pages of Carrie out of a wastebasket and tell him to go on. The research pool contradicts itself here, one lens placing the meeting in Burton Hatlen's writing workshop. The library is the version both Wikipedia articles carry.
suggested_refs: Raymond H. Fogler Library, University of Maine, Orono

stops.name: Worumbo Mill, Lisbon Falls, the basement
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction: the summer is not fixed by any reachable source; the pool's original c. 1965 is not supportable and c. 1969-1970 is the better placing
stops.campa: In Lisbon Falls he takes a summer job at the Worumbo textile mill, working the floor of a building where the machines never entirely stop. He will say afterward that he saw rats the size of cats in the basement under the dye house. The story Graveyard Shift comes out of that basement and that night shift. The dating is unsettled and the current Wikipedia article on the story carries no background section at all, so the summer is placed by King's own later accounts rather than by a document.
suggested_refs: Worumbo Mill, Lisbon Falls; King's introductions to Night Shift on the origin of Graveyard Shift

stops.name: Orono, the degree and the first daughter
stops.date_confidence: attested for the year; the month is conventional
stops.campa: King takes his Bachelor of Arts in English, with a teaching certificate, and the same year his daughter Naomi Rachel is born. He is twenty-two, a father, a graduate, and unable to find a classroom that will hire him. The stories he places in men's magazines pay in the low hundreds. Between the degree and the first novel lie four years in which the only measurable fact about the career is that he keeps typing, and the only measurable fact about the life is that it gets more expensive every year.
suggested_refs: University of Maine commencement records, 1970

segments.name: The Laundry, the Trailer, the Telegram

stops.name: New Franklin Laundry, Bangor, feeding the machines
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction: the job is attested only in King's own accounts and the coordinates given are generic downtown Bangor, not the laundry's Hammond Street site
stops.campa: With no classroom to go to, King takes work at an industrial laundry, feeding motel sheets and restaurant tablecloths and hospital linen into machines that could take an arm off a tired man. The hours are long, the work is dangerous and stupefying, and the tedium of a machine floor enters the fiction and stays there. The job is well attested in his own interviews and in On Writing; it is absent from the Wikipedia article the research cited, and is therefore carried here as his own testimony rather than as documentation.
suggested_refs: New Franklin Laundry, Hammond Street, Bangor
sources: Stephen King, On Writing: A Memoir of the Craft

stops.name: Orono, the wedding
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction: the date comes from the Tabitha King article and is not confirmed against a civil record here
stops.campa: Stephen King and Tabitha Spruce marry near the university where they met. She takes extra shifts at a doughnut counter while he writes at night; between them they have two small children, no money, and a mounting conviction that the writing is not a hobby they will grow out of. The house changes, the publisher changes, the body is broken and rebuilt, the addictions arrive and are put down, and the marriage made here is still standing fifty years later.
suggested_refs: Marriage record of Stephen King and Tabitha Spruce, Orono, January 1971

stops.name: Hampden Academy, teaching English
stops.date_confidence: attested for 1971-1973; the September start is conventional
stops.campa: King is hired to teach English at Hampden Academy. The salary is small and the marking is endless, and what the job actually buys him is evenings and summers. He writes in the hours the school leaves over, submits to magazines, and spikes the rejection slips on a nail in the wall until the nail will no longer hold them. Two years here. The teacher who cannot place a novel will, within four years of walking out of this building, be the best-selling novelist in the United States and never take a salaried job again.
suggested_refs: Hampden Academy, Hampden, Maine

stops.name: Hermon, the trailer and the laundry room
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction: the pool gives 1972-1973 without a month
stops.campa: The family lives in a rented trailer outside Bangor. King writes on a child's desk wedged into the laundry room, typing between the washer and the dryer, and after three pages about a bullied girl with a telekinetic gift he throws the thing out. Tabitha takes the pages out of the wastebasket, reads them, and says she wants to know what happens next. He finishes it. The manuscript is called Carrie, and the room it is written in is smaller than the bathroom of the house it eventually buys.
suggested_refs: The King family trailer, Hermon, Maine, where Carrie was drafted

stops.name: Doubleday, New York, the manuscript taken
stops.date_confidence: attested for the month; the coordinates are a generic Midtown pin, not a Doubleday address
stops.campa: Bill Thompson, an editor at Doubleday, accepts Carrie and gets the hardcover advance raised from fifteen hundred dollars to twenty-five hundred. The transforming money arrives later, when New American Library pays four hundred thousand dollars for the mass-market paperback rights and half of it is the author's. The telegram reaches a rented trailer in Hermon where a schoolteacher is waiting. Two hundred thousand is the figure repeated everywhere; four hundred thousand is the sale, and the research pool corrects the conflation.
suggested_refs: The New American Library paperback rights sale for Carrie, 1973

stops.name: Durham, the mother's death
stops.date_confidence: attested; one research lens misplaces this death to 1975 beside 'Salem's Lot, following loose phrasing in the Wikipedia article
stops.campa: Nellie Ruth Pillsbury King dies of uterine cancer in December 1973. Her son has sold his first novel and she does not live to see it in a shop; he has read her portions of the draft aloud. The woman who moved two boys across six states on other people's charity dies four months before the book that ends the family's poverty is published. The contradiction between the two research lenses is left standing here: one dates the death to 1975, the other to 1973, and the publication calendar agrees with 1973.
suggested_refs: Nellie Ruth Pillsbury King, died 18 December 1973, Durham, Maine

stops.name: New York, Carrie in hardcover
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: Doubleday publishes Carrie on the fifth of April 1974 in a first printing of thirty thousand copies, a modest run for a first novel by nobody in particular. It is a high school story: a girl humiliated in a locker room brings a town down on itself. It sells slowly in hardcover and enormously in paperback, and by the time Brian De Palma films it in 1976 the author is a household name. The teaching certificate is never used again. He enters the line of American gothic that runs back through Edgar Allan Poe.
suggested_refs: Carrie, Doubleday first edition, 5 April 1974

stops.name: Boulder, the change of air
stops.date_confidence: attested for the year; the month is conventional and one lens misdates the move to 1975
stops.campa: With the paperback money in hand and his mother buried, King takes the family out of Maine to Colorado, renting in Boulder. He begins the long book about a plague that empties America, the novel that becomes The Stand, in a state that holds none of his own history. The distance from Maine is deliberate and it is temporary. He is back within two years, and after Colorado he never again writes at length about any ground but the one he grew up standing on.
suggested_refs: Boulder, Colorado, the King family rental of 1974-1975

stops.name: The Stanley Hotel, Room 217
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: The Kings drive up to Estes Park and check into the Stanley on the night before it closes for the season. They are nearly the only guests in the building. Dinner is served to one table in an empty dining room and the orchestra plays for nobody. He walks the corridors, finds room 217, pulls back the curtain on a claw-footed tub, and the question arrives. That night he dreams of his three-year-old son running screaming through the halls pursued by a fire hose. By morning he has The Shining, entire, before a word of it is written.
stops.quote: What if somebody died here? At that moment, I knew I had a book.
stops.quote_source: Stephen King on the night of 30 October 1974 at the Stanley Hotel, as reported in Wikipedia's article on The Shining; the pink-curtain and claw-foot details belong to the article's narration, not to King's quoted words
suggested_refs: The Stanley Hotel, Estes Park, Colorado, room 217
sources: Stanley Hotel history and King interviews

stops.name: Auburn, The Stand finished
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction: the year is attested, the month is not
stops.campa: The family returns east to Auburn, and here King finishes the manuscript of The Stand. On the seventeenth of October 1975 Doubleday publishes 'Salem's Lot, a vampire novel about a Maine town that empties house by house while its neighbours decline to notice anything. He has three novels written and two published, and he is twenty-eight. The Stand is cut hard for length and restored fifteen years later at the author's insistence, at which point it becomes the longest book most of his readers have ever finished.
suggested_refs: 'Salem's Lot, Doubleday, 17 October 1975

segments.name: Orrington and the Ground Behind the House

stops.name: University of Maine, Orono, writer-in-residence
stops.date_confidence: attested for 1977-1979; the month is conventional
stops.campa: King returns to the university that gave him a scholarship, this time to teach creative writing. The Shining is published the same year; his third child, Owen Philip, is born; the family takes a short residence in England and comes home early. The appointment brings them back to the Orono and Bangor country for good. He is teaching in the rooms where Burton Hatlen taught him, seven years after taking his degree, on the strength of three novels written in a laundry room and a series of rented houses.
suggested_refs: University of Maine writer-in-residence appointment, 1977-1979

stops.name: Orrington, the road that kills things
stops.date_confidence: attested for the year of residence; the month is conventional
stops.campa: The family rents a house in Orrington on a road the trucks take fast. Animals die on that road with regularity, and the children of the town have cut a cemetery for them into the woods behind the houses. King's daughter's cat is killed on the highway and buried there. Then his son runs toward the road and he catches him. Out of the road, the cat, and that lunge comes the premise. The essay that queues him here reads the same decade against the Diffie-Hellman key exchange and the RSA work that follows it.
suggested_refs: The Orrington rental beside Maine Route 15, 1979

stops.name: The pet cemetery behind the rental
stops.date_confidence: attested: the first draft is finished in May 1979
stops.campa: Past the trees the children's graves are marked with boards and bicycle reflectors, and the hand-lettered sign spells the word wrong. Beyond them in the novel he sets a Mi'kmaq burying ground that returns what is put into it, changed. He finishes the draft, finds it so bleak that he locks the manuscript in a drawer, and leaves it there for four years before Doubleday publishes it in 1983, calling it the one that scared him the most.
stops.quote_source: Pet Sematary (Doubleday, 1983), the words attached to Jud Crandall's warning
suggested_refs: The children's pet cemetery in the woods at Orrington, Maine

stops.name: 47 West Broadway, the bat gate
stops.date_confidence: attested for the year of purchase; the month is not fixed, and the sources conflict on whether the house is of 1856 or 1858
stops.campa: King buys the William Arnold House on West Broadway in Bangor, an Italianate mansion of 1856, and hangs on it a wrought-iron fence worked with bats and spiders. The gate is his own addition to a historic structure: a nineteenth-century merchant's house given a horror writer's grammar in iron. It becomes the most photographed address in Maine and a permanent destination for readers, who stand at the fence and take the same picture. The research pool contradicts itself on the date, 1856 in the article body against 1858 in a photograph caption.
suggested_refs: The William Arnold House, 47 West Broadway, Whitney Park Historic District, Bangor

stops.name: Bangor, the storm drains and the making of Derry
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction: the research places the work between 1980 and 1985 without fixing a start
stops.campa: He walks the city he now lives in and reads its Victorian storm drains, the canal running buried under the streets, the flood that took part of the town. Out of Bangor he builds Derry: the same bridges, the same standpipe on the hill, the same water moving underneath everything, and in the water a thing that wears a clown. The fictional town is not a disguise for the real one. It is the real one with its drainage made legible. He works on the book for five years and lives inside the map the entire time.
suggested_refs: The Bangor storm drain and canal system; the Thomas Hill Standpipe

stops.name: New York, Pet Sematary published
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: Doubleday publishes Pet Sematary on the fourteenth of November 1983, three hundred and seventy-four pages in hardcover. King has said the book frightened him more than anything else he wrote and that he nearly left it in the drawer; it goes out in part to settle a contract. It takes a World Fantasy Award nomination in 1984. In French it is titled Simetierre, carrying the child's misspelling across the language. The word on a sign in the woods behind an Orrington rental is now the title of a book in a dozen countries.
stops.quote: On a couple of occasions I've shocked myself. Pet Sematary was appalling when it first came out on to the page.
stops.quote_source: Tim Adams, 'Interview: Stephen King', The Guardian, 14 September 2000, cited from Wikiquote's raw wikitext; the Guardian domain refused all fetches this session, so the primary article was not read directly
suggested_refs: Pet Sematary, Doubleday first edition, 14 November 1983; the French Simetierre

stops.name: Kezar Lake, Lovell, the summer house
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction: the acquisition date is not confirmed by any source reached; regional press and fan accounts place it in the 1980s
stops.campa: The Kings take a summer house on Kezar Lake in Lovell, in the western Maine hill country near the New Hampshire line, and keep it for decades. The lake towns of that corner of the state recur across the fiction under other names, borrowed water and borrowed roads. The purchase date is fixed by nothing reachable and is carried as reconstruction. What is certain is that the family is established on this water well before the century turns, and that a stretch of road near this house will one day come very close to killing him.
suggested_refs: The King property on Kezar Lake, Lovell, Maine
sources: regional press and fan-site accounts; acquisition date unconfirmed

stops.name: Viking Press, New York, It
stops.date_confidence: attested; one research lens dates the publication to 1987, which is the award year rather than the publication year
stops.campa: Viking publishes It on the fifteenth of September 1986, five years of writing begun in 1980, from an idea King traces to a wooden footbridge he crossed in Boulder in 1978. Seven children fight a thing living under their town and come back as adults to finish the job. It becomes one of his longest and best-selling novels and takes the British Fantasy Award, the August Derleth, in 1987. The two research lenses collapse the award year into the publication year and separate them; the separation is the correct one.
stops.quote: Eddie discovered one of his childhood's great truths. Grownups are the real monsters, he thought.
stops.quote_source: It (Viking, 1986), free indirect narration through Eddie Kaspbrak, quoted verbatim on Goodreads' Stephen King author-quotes page
suggested_refs: It, Viking Press first edition, 15 September 1986

stops.name: Bangor, the intervention
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction: the intervention is placed at about 1987 and the completion of treatment at 1988, neither with a documented date
stops.campa: Tabitha King confronts her husband about the drinking and the drugs and puts the choice to him plainly: treatment, or the end of the marriage. He has written years of books he will afterward say he cannot remember writing. Treatment is completed, by the research pool's reconstruction, in 1988. The same year his old university awards him an honorary doctorate, a date the accounts carry variably. Everything published after this point is written sober, and at no moment in the transition does the output stop or even visibly slow.
suggested_refs: The 1987 family intervention, recounted in On Writing
sources: Stephen King, On Writing: A Memoir of the Craft

stops.name: Mount Hope Cemetery, Bangor, the film goes into the ground
stops.date_confidence: attested for the year of the film; the shooting months are not fixed here
stops.campa: Mary Lambert films Pet Sematary in Maine from King's own screenplay, basing production in Ellsworth, putting the Creed house in Hancock, and shooting the graveyard scenes in Mount Hope Cemetery, a working burial ground opened in 1834. The Mi'kmaq ground is a hilltop near Sedgwick and the approach to it an abandoned granite quarry on Mount Desert Island. A real cemetery of the actual dead lends its stones to a story about the dead who are brought back and should not have been.
suggested_refs: Mount Hope Cemetery, Bangor, founded 1834; Pet Sematary (1989) Maine locations

stops.name: Bangor, Needful Things and the first sober book
stops.date_confidence: attested for the year; the month is not fixed here
stops.campa: Needful Things is published in 1991, the first novel King writes after getting sober, and he sets it in Castle Rock and then destroys the town at the end of it. Gerald's Game and Dolores Claiborne follow in 1992, two books about women left alone with a man's violence, written by a man who has recently stopped being the problem in his own house. The rate of production does not fall. What changes is that he can now give an account, afterward, of what he was doing while he did it.
suggested_refs: Needful Things, 1991, the last Castle Rock novel of the original sequence

segments.name: Lovell, the Van, the Book on Writing

stops.name: New York, The Man in the Black Suit and the serial
stops.date_confidence: attested for the Halloween 1994 issue; the O. Henry Award follows in 1996
stops.campa: The New Yorker prints The Man in the Black Suit in its Halloween issue of 1994, and the story takes the O. Henry Award in 1996. The same year the film of The Shawshank Redemption reaches cinemas, out of a novella in Different Seasons that nobody had thought to file under horror. In 1996 he publishes The Green Mile in six monthly paperback instalments in the manner of Dickens, and every one of them enters the best-seller list. The magazines that would not review him now commission him.
stops.quote: Get busy living or get busy dying.
stops.quote_source: Different Seasons (Viking, 1982), novella 'Rita Hayworth and Shawshank Redemption'; the line given to Andy Dufresne
suggested_refs: The New Yorker, Halloween issue 1994; The Green Mile, six-part serial, 1996

stops.name: Casey Key, the winter house
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction: no purchase date is confirmed; the residence rests on press profiles, and the Wikipedia article on Casey Key does not mention King at all
stops.campa: The Kings take a winter house on Casey Key, a barrier island south of Sarasota, and begin splitting the year between Florida sand and Maine snow. The arrangement holds for decades and turns up in nearly every profile written of him afterward. Nothing in the reachable record fixes when it began. The evidence here is thinner than for anything else in this record: journalists reporting an address, without a deed, a date, or a municipal record behind them. The claim is carried as reported and not as documented.
suggested_refs: Casey Key, Sarasota County, Florida
sources: author profiles and interviews; purchase date unconfirmed

stops.name: Scribner, New York, Bag of Bones
stops.date_confidence: attested; the awards belong to 1999, not to 1998 as one research lens has it
stops.campa: Bag of Bones is published on the twenty-second of September 1998, King's first book with Scribner after two decades at Doubleday and Viking. It is a ghost story about a novelist who cannot write, told by a man who has never once been unable to. It takes the Bram Stoker Award and the British Fantasy Award, both in 1999. He has by this point published more than forty books and changed publishing house exactly once, and he is fifty-one years old with the largest readership of any living novelist.
stops.quote: Humor is almost always anger with its makeup on, I think, but in little towns the makeup tends to be thin.
stops.quote_source: Bag of Bones (Scribner, 1998), ch. 8, p. 148, narrator Mike Noonan; verified against Wikiquote raw wikitext and Goodreads quote search
suggested_refs: Bag of Bones, Scribner, 22 September 1998

stops.name: Route 5, North Lovell, the van
stops.date_confidence: attested for the date; the pin is moved north onto Route 5 above Center Lovell, the research coordinates having fallen southwest of the village and off the road
stops.campa: On the nineteenth of June 1999 King is walking the shoulder of Maine State Route 5 near his Lovell house when a Dodge Caravan leaves the road and strikes him. The driver, Bryan Smith, has been reaching for a dog loose in the back of the van. King is thrown into a ditch with a collapsed lung, a shattered hip, and a leg broken in several places, and faces years of surgery. He has written a novelist crippled by a reader and a writer's legs destroyed with a sledgehammer. The road takes its turn at him.
stops.quote: killed by a character out of one of my own novels
stops.quote_source: King's later remark on the accident, that it was 'almost funny' to be 'killed by a character out of one of my own novels'; quoted as fragments because the research pool preserves only the fragments
suggested_refs: Maine State Route 5, North Lovell, site of the 19 June 1999 accident

stops.name: Center Lovell, writing at forty minutes a session
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction: King's own account in On Writing, not corroborated independently here
stops.campa: Through the second half of 1999 and into 2000 King recovers at the family's western Maine lake property, working in sessions that leave him soaked and shaking and end when the hip will take no more. He describes them in On Writing as agony and as the thing that saved him. The manuscript on the desk is the memoir itself, begun before the van and finished after it, so that the book about how to write acquires, halfway through its length, a man learning again how to sit upright in a chair.
stops.quote: Writing is not life, but I think that sometimes it can be a way back to life.
stops.quote_source: On Writing: A Memoir of the Craft (Scribner, 2000), written after the 1999 accident
suggested_refs: On Writing: A Memoir of the Craft, the post-accident chapters
sources: Stephen King, On Writing: A Memoir of the Craft

stops.name: Scribner, New York, On Writing
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction: the year is attested, the publication month is not fixed in the research pool
stops.campa: On Writing: A Memoir of the Craft is published, half an autobiography compressed to the bone and half a manual: read a lot, write a lot, cut the adverbs, draft with the door shut and revise with it open. It takes the Bram Stoker and Locus awards for nonfiction and becomes the book most often put into the hands of people who want to start. The same year he issues Riding the Bullet directly as an electronic book and it is downloaded more than five hundred thousand times, before anyone has settled what that means.
stops.quote: The road to hell is paved with adverbs.
stops.quote_source: On Writing: A Memoir of the Craft (Scribner, 2000), craft section
suggested_refs: On Writing, Scribner, 2000; Riding the Bullet, Simon and Schuster electronic edition, 2000

segments.name: The Late Honors and the Living Author

stops.name: New York, the National Book Awards medal
stops.date_confidence: attested for the date; the venue for the 2003 ceremony is not independently confirmed in the sources reached
stops.campa: King receives the Medal for Distinguished Contribution to American Letters at the National Book Awards. The award is contested in public, before and after the ceremony, by critics holding that a writer of horror paperbacks does not belong on the same platform as the year's literary honorees. He accepts it. Twenty-nine years earlier the same country's shops had put Carrie on a wire spinner rack beside the cash register, thirty thousand copies, and left it to find out whether anyone would buy it.
suggested_refs: National Book Foundation, Medal for Distinguished Contribution to American Letters, 2003

stops.name: Harvard Book Store, Cambridge, the queue
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: King reads and signs at an independent bookshop in Cambridge, one stop among hundreds of appearances punctuating five decades of publication. It is the ordinary machinery of a working novelist's life, and it is the reason his movements can be tracked so closely at all. Historical travelers from earlier centuries must usually be reconstructed from charters and consular dispatches. King's movements are recorded by bookshops: ticketed, dated, photographed by the people who stood in line for them.
suggested_refs: Harvard Book Store, Massachusetts Avenue, Cambridge

stops.name: The White House, the National Medal of Arts
stops.date_confidence: attested for the ceremony; the medal itself is the 2014 award, and the two research lenses give the two different years without either being wrong
stops.campa: President Obama hangs the National Medal of Arts on Stephen King, citing his command of the short story and the novel and his habit of putting ordinary people into extraordinary circumstances. The sources give two years and both are correct about different things: the medal is the 2014 award and the ceremony is the tenth of September 2015. He is sixty-seven, holds the National Book Foundation's medal and the nation's arts medal, and is still shelved in bookshops under horror.
suggested_refs: National Endowment for the Arts, National Medal of Arts, 2014 class, conferred September 2015
sources: National Endowment for the Arts records

stops.name: Bangor Public Library, the money going back
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction: the research gives the patronage only as ongoing, with no dated act
stops.campa: A large share of the money goes back into the city that supplied Derry. The Stephen and Tabitha King Foundation funds Maine libraries, schools, and local nonprofits; the radio stations WZON and WKIT are owned by a company owned by the novelist; Tabitha King sits on the board of the Bangor Public Library. The attribution is uneven and is left uneven here. The station ownership is documented in the city's own article; the library service is attested for Tabitha and reconstructed for Stephen, whose name the research attached without a source.
suggested_refs: Bangor Public Library, 145 Harlow Street; Zone Radio Corporation, WZON and WKIT

stops.name: Bangor, You Like It Darker and no grave at all
stops.date_confidence: attested for the month of publication; the day is not fixed in the research pool
stops.campa: Holly appears in September 2023 and You Like It Darker in May 2024, entering the fiction list at number one. The adaptations run without a break: It in 2017 among the highest-grossing horror films ever released, Castle Rock on television from 2018 to 2019 stitching the Maine towns into one country, Pet Sematary filmed again in 2019 and given a prequel in 2023. The author is alive and working. There is no tomb, no monument, and no documented statue, and the afterlife section of this entry has nothing to visit.
stops.quote: Books are a uniquely portable magic.
stops.quote_source: On Writing: A Memoir of the Craft (Scribner, 2000), quoted verbatim on Goodreads' Stephen King author-quotes page
suggested_refs: You Like It Darker, Scribner, May 2024; the 2017-2023 adaptation cycle
